cases.claim: The description is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it, and make it a little 'pushy' to combat undertriggering.
cases.prompt: You are authoring a new agent skill called `pdf-form-filler` that fills the fields of a fillable PDF form from a supplied field-to-value mapping and then flattens the result so the fields are no longer editable. Write ONLY the `description:` value that will go in this skill's YAML frontmatter. Output the description text by itself (one paragraph, plain text) with no other commentary.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim that a skill's frontmatter description is the primary triggering mechanism and must combine WHAT the skill does with SPECIFIC when-to-use contexts, phrased so the model reliably reaches for it. Checkable criteria: (a) the description states what the skill does (fills and flattens fillable PDF forms from a field mapping); (b) it enumerates concrete, specific contexts/trigger phrases for WHEN to use it (e.g. a user has a fillable/AcroForm PDF to populate, wants to auto-fill form fields from data, needs to flatten a completed PDF, mentions form templates) rather than only naming the capability once; (c) it is written to encourage triggering / counter undertriggering (e.g. 'use this whenever ...', covers cases where the user needs it but does not literally say 'fill a PDF form'). SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic description that does all three scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary in trigger coverage — it names several distinct realistic phrasings/contexts including at least one where the user would not literally say 'fill a form'. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP rules: if the description states only what the skill does with no specific when-to-use contexts, cap at 0.3. If all when-to-use guidance is generic ('use when relevant') rather than concrete, cap at 0.5. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct flaw (no what/does statement; no trigger contexts at all; not written to encourage triggering; includes body-style instructions instead of a description; rambling far beyond a description).

cases.claim: Skills use three-level progressive disclosure (metadata ~100 words / SKILL.md body <500 lines / bundled resources on demand); keep SKILL.md under 500 lines, move detail into reference files, and point to them clearly.
cases.prompt: A SKILL.md for a skill called `data-cleaning` has grown to about 900 lines because it inlines detailed step-by-step cleaning recipes for four formats (CSV, Excel, JSON, and Parquet) plus a 200-line troubleshooting appendix, all in the one file. In plain text, describe concretely how you would restructure this skill's files so it follows good progressive-disclosure practice. Be specific about what content lives where and how the pieces connect.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim of three-level progressive disclosure and the guidance to keep SKILL.md under ~500 lines by moving detail into reference files with clear pointers. Checkable criteria: (a) explains the layered loading model — frontmatter metadata (name+description, always in context) / SKILL.md body (loaded when the skill triggers, keep it lean, ideally <500 lines) / bundled resources loaded only as needed; (b) moves the four per-format recipes out of the body into separate reference files (e.g. references/csv.md, excel.md, json.md, parquet.md) and moves the troubleshooting appendix out too; (c) keeps in SKILL.md the shared/high-level workflow plus selection logic, with explicit POINTERS telling the model when to read each reference file. Bonus-worthy: recommends a table of contents for large (>300-line) reference files. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic answer that does (a)-(c) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it explains WHY progressive disclosure matters (context economy: the body should not force irrelevant format detail into context) and gives concrete pointer wording. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional (rare). CAP rules: if the answer does not move the per-format detail into separate reference files with pointers from SKILL.md, cap at 0.3. If it keeps everything in one file (e.g. only reorders sections), cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct flaw (omits the three-level model; leaves the troubleshooting appendix inline; no pointers/guidance on when to read each reference; confuses the metadata/body/resources layers).

cases.claim: Define the output format explicitly, giving an exact template the model should follow, and include worked examples (input -> output).
cases.prompt: You are writing the SKILL.md for a skill that converts a developer's rough, unstructured release notes into a single standardized changelog entry. Write the section of the SKILL.md that specifies the required OUTPUT FORMAT. It should give the model an exact template to follow and at least one worked example. Output just that section in Markdown.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim that a skill should define its output format with an exact, reusable template plus worked examples. Checkable criteria: (a) provides an explicit, concrete template with a fixed structure (e.g. a labeled changelog entry: version/date heading, then grouped change types like Added/Changed/Fixed, entry lines) presented AS a template to follow, not as vague prose description; (b) the template is reusable/general (placeholders or clearly generic fields), not just one hard-coded example masquerading as a format; (c) includes at least one worked example demonstrating the transformation from rough input to the formatted output. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic section that does (a)-(c) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it clearly separates the reusable template from the example (e.g. an Input/Output-style example) so both a spec and a demonstration are present and unambiguous. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional (rare). CAP rules: if the section gives no concrete template (only describes the format in prose), cap at 0.3. If it gives a template but no worked example, cap at 0.5. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct flaw (template is actually a single hard-coded instance with no generality; example does not show the input-to-output transformation; format is internally inconsistent).

cases.claim: Prefer theory-of-mind 'why' instructions that explain reasoning over heavy-handed all-caps MUSTs/ALWAYS/NEVER, while still preserving the underlying requirements.
cases.prompt:
The following instructions from a code-review skill are written in a rigid, all-caps style. Rewrite them so they follow good skill-writing style — explaining the reasoning behind each requirement so the model understands why it matters — while still preserving every underlying requirement. Output only the rewritten instructions.

---
YOU MUST ALWAYS check for SQL injection in EVERY database query. NEVER approve code that concatenates user input into SQL. YOU MUST ALWAYS flag any function longer than 50 lines. NEVER skip checking error handling. YOU MUST ALWAYS leave at least one positive comment.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim that skill instructions should favor 'why'-based, theory-of-mind framing over heavy all-caps MUST/ALWAYS/NEVER mandates, WITHOUT dropping the underlying requirements. Checkable criteria: (a) the rewrite removes the heavy-handed all-caps mandate style (no wall of MUST/ALWAYS/NEVER) and reads as reasoned guidance; (b) it explains the WHY behind the requirements (e.g. why concatenating user input into SQL is dangerous, why very long functions are a reviewability/maintainability concern, why a positive comment helps the author act on feedback); (c) it PRESERVES every original requirement — SQL-injection/concatenation check, flagging overly long functions, checking error handling, and including at least one positive comment. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic rewrite that does (a)-(c) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — the 'why' framing is genuinely instructive (gives the model useful judgment, e.g. that the 50-line threshold is a heuristic prompting a closer look, not a hard rule) rather than a mechanical restatement. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional (rare). CAP rules: if the rewrite keeps the heavy all-caps MUST/ALWAYS/NEVER style, cap at 0.3. If it drops any of the original requirements, cap at 0.4. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct flaw (no reasoning added for a requirement; softens a requirement into optionality when it should remain expected; introduces new unrelated rules).

cases.claim: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant — one reference file per variant with the SKILL.md holding shared workflow and selection logic pointing to the right file, so only the relevant reference is read.
cases.prompt: A skill called `iac-linter` needs to support three infrastructure-as-code frameworks — Terraform, CloudFormation, and Pulumi — each with substantially different linting rules. In plain text, describe the file/directory layout you would use and how the SKILL.md should route to the correct framework. Include the directory tree.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim about organizing multi-domain skills by variant, with per-variant reference files and SKILL.md-level selection/pointers. Checkable criteria: (a) proposes a references/ directory with one file per framework (e.g. references/terraform.md, references/cloudformation.md, references/pulumi.md); (b) keeps the SKILL.md focused on the shared workflow plus SELECTION/routing logic (how to detect or choose which framework applies) that points the model to the matching reference file; (c) makes clear that only the relevant reference file is read/loaded rather than all three inlined into the body; (d) shows a concrete directory tree. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic answer that does (a)-(d) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it explains WHY this structure helps (avoids loading two irrelevant frameworks' rules into context) and gives concrete routing/pointer wording the SKILL.md would use. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional (rare). CAP rules: if the answer inlines all three frameworks' rules into SKILL.md or otherwise fails to separate variants into their own reference files, cap at 0.3. If there is no selection/routing logic connecting SKILL.md to the right file, cap at 0.5. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct flaw (no directory tree; framework files not clearly one-per-variant; implies all references load every time).

cases.claim: A good SKILL.md combines a triggering frontmatter description (what + specific when-to-use contexts), a lean well-structured body, an explicit output-format template with an example, and reasoned 'why' instructions rather than rigid all-caps MUSTs.
cases.prompt: Draft a complete SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter plus Markdown body) for a skill named `sql-migration-writer` that generates a reversible database migration — an 'up' script and a matching 'down' script — from a plain-English schema-change request (for example, 'add a nullable email column to the users table'). This skill needs no bundled resources; keep everything self-contained in the one file. Output the full SKILL.md.
cases.rubric: Grade holistically against the claim that a strong SKILL.md integrates a triggering description, a lean structured body, an output template with an example, and reasoned instruction tone. Checkable criteria: (a) valid frontmatter with `name` (sql-migration-writer) and a `description` that states what the skill does AND lists specific when-to-use contexts (user requests a schema change / needs a migration / add/drop/alter columns or tables / wants a reversible up+down migration) and is written to encourage triggering; (b) the body defines the OUTPUT FORMAT with an explicit template for the reversible migration (an up section and a matching down section) and includes at least one worked example (e.g. the nullable-email request -> up/down SQL); (c) the body emphasizes reversibility reasoning — the 'down' must undo the 'up' — and is written in reasoned 'why' style rather than a wall of all-caps MUST/ALWAYS/NEVER; (d) the body is coherently structured and reasonably concise (no bloat, single self-contained file). SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic SKILL.md that does (a)-(d) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — the description has notably strong trigger coverage AND the migration template handles a subtlety of reversibility (e.g. that some operations are not cleanly reversible and how to handle/flag that). Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP rules: if there is no real triggering description (only a bare capability line with no when-to-use contexts), cap at 0.4. If the body gives no explicit output template for the up/down migration, cap at 0.4. If it has no worked example, cap at 0.6. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct flaw (missing frontmatter field; all-caps MUST-heavy tone; no reversibility/down reasoning; disorganized or bloated body).

cases.claim: All when-to-use info belongs in the frontmatter description (the trigger), not a body section; the SKILL.md body should stay lean via progressive disclosure; and instructions should use reasoned 'why' framing rather than heavy all-caps MUSTs.
cases.prompt:
Critique the following SKILL.md and give concrete, specific fixes. Point out what is wrong and show how to fix the most important problems (including a rewritten description). Output your critique and fixes in plain text.

---
name: chart-maker
description: Formats data.

# Chart Maker

## When to use this skill
Use this skill when the user wants a bar chart, a line chart, a pie chart, or any other kind of chart, or mentions plotting, graphing, or visualizing numbers, or has a CSV of metrics they want to see visually.

## Instructions
YOU MUST ALWAYS use a colorblind-safe palette. NEVER use red-green together. YOU MUST ALWAYS label every axis. [... followed by ~600 lines that inline full, separate step-by-step recipes for Matplotlib, Plotly, and D3 ...]
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claims that (1) when-to-use info is the job of the frontmatter description (the trigger), not a body section, and the description here is far too weak; (2) a ~600-line body inlining three libraries' recipes violates progressive disclosure and should be split into per-library reference files with pointers; (3) the all-caps MUST/NEVER instruction style should be reframed with reasoning. Checkable criteria: (a) identifies that the rich when-to-use content is stranded in a body '## When to use' section while the actual `description` ('Formats data.') is uselessly vague and not a real trigger — and that when-to-use belongs IN the description; (b) provides a concrete rewritten description that states what the skill does AND folds in the specific when-to-use contexts (and is written to trigger reliably); (c) flags the ~600-line monolith and recommends moving the per-library recipes (Matplotlib/Plotly/D3) into separate reference files with selection pointers from SKILL.md (progressive disclosure); (d) flags the all-caps MUST/NEVER tone and recommends reasoned 'why' framing while keeping the requirements. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic critique that hits (a)-(d) scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — the rewritten description is genuinely strong (concrete trigger phrasings, counters undertriggering) AND it explains the underlying WHY for each fix. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional (rare). CAP rules: if the critique does not identify the core description/trigger problem (weak description + when-to-use misplaced in the body), cap at 0.3. If it offers no concrete rewritten description, cap at 0.5. Subtract ~0.2 for each of the other two issues (progressive-disclosure/body-split; all-caps tone) it misses, and ~0.2 for any clearly wrong advice.
